#591. A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history

In the hills of north-west Morocco, overlooking the river that gives the site its name, research at Oued Beht is bringing to light a previously unknown chapter of the region’s past. The discovery of a substantial built structure suggests that, during the second millennium BC, communities in north-west Africa were actively shaping their environment. They were also engaging in broader networks of interaction across the Mediterranean world.

Previous research by the Oued Beht Archaeological Project had already brought to light what is likely the earliest and largest agricultural complex ever discovered in Africa outside the Nile Valley. It dates to around 5,400 to 4,900 years ago. New excavations carried out in 2023 – in which we took part – have now deepened our understanding of the site.

Our new study shows how we uncovered the earliest known large-scale construction of a probably defensive nature in north Africa beyond the Nile Valley. It’s about 4,000 to 3,500 years old.

It’s not known exactly what threats these wall-like structures were designed to counter. They likely relate to increasing competition over land, resources, and possibly control of movement through the landscape, rather than to “invaders”. Constructions like these suggest communities felt the need to protect themselves or assert power over strategic locations.

This discovery pushes back the evidence for organized defensive architecture in the Maghreb and suggests that societies in this region at this time were more complex and structured than previously believed.

Our study also reveals how the ridge of Oued Beht would become a focal point again in the medieval period, during the 11th to 13th centuries AD. The same defensive structure was rebuilt, a hamlet or farm was established on a nearby hilltop, and people were buried in a cemetery between the two areas.

Together these findings provide rare archaeological insights into rural communities during both prehistoric and medieval times. They help us understand how societies developed and maintained themselves in a region too often left out of the history books.

For a long time, the later prehistory of north Africa’s Maghreb region (the Mediterranean countries of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia) has been poorly understood. Compared with neighboring areas such as Iberia in south-western Europe or Athens in the eastern Mediterranean, archaeological evidence was often fragmentary. In the last few years this has changed completely.

Excavations at Oued Beht have revealed a large concentration of human activity spread across at least ten hectares. The earliest major phase dates to the mid-fourth and early third millennia BC, or the Final Neolithic period.

Environmental evidence from plant and animal remains in the prehistoric era indicates a farming community cultivating crops such as barley and wheat. They also exploited wild plants and kept livestock.

The site was also an important center of craft production. Thousands of polished stone axes and other tools have been discovered, along with finely made pottery, sometimes decorated with painted patterns.

It’s still uncertain whether prehistoric Oued Beht functioned as a permanent village, a seasonal center, or something less familiar. But it was clearly a major focus in the landscape of north-west Morocco.

The presence of potentially ancient earthworks and walls had been noted since the 1930s. The French archaeologist Armand Ruhlmann first documented a configuration of three walls, with the fourth side protected by the natural scarp of the ridge, describing a defensive éperon barré (barred spur). Their precise nature and date remained uncertain until now.

New excavations have clarified the existence of a multi-phase ditch, rampart and wall built across a narrow section of the Oued Beht ridge between the river and a ravine. This cut off and protected the ridge’s southern tip.

Radiocarbon dating of deposits associated with these structures gave us the timelines in our study.

They place its original construction at a time equivalent to the Bronze Age of the remaining western Mediterranean. This makes it the earliest confirmed defensive construction in north Africa outside Egypt.

This structure raises important questions about the society that built it. Building an embankment and ditch system required planning, coordination and the mobilization of labor. This suggests a community capable of organizing complex construction initiatives.

During the earlier Neolithic phase, activity at Oued Beht focused on the larger and more open northern area of the site. By the period of our new study, focus had shifted to the narrower, more defensible southern ridge. This may reflect a shift in settlement strategies.

The second millennium BC was a dynamic period across the Mediterranean. In southern Iberia, Argaric societies (about 2200-1550 BC) in today’s Europe were developing complex, often hilltop settlements. They were characterized by planned architecture, advanced metallurgy (especially bronze production), and marked social hierarchies visible in burial practices. These communities often constructed fortified sites, and strategically located settlements controlling surrounding territories.

Increasing evidence suggests that communities in north-west Africa were connected to wider Mediterranean networks. This includes today’s Spain and Portugal. The discoveries at Oued Beht indicate that the Maghreb was not isolated. It participated in broader processes shaping the western Mediterranean.

The defensive system at the site may reflect wider transformations in social organization and regional interaction. There may have been growing competition over resources, control of movement, and more formalized leadership structures.

The discoveries at Oued Beht highlight how much remains to be learned about the deep history of north Africa. The defensive wall shows that communities here were able to coordinate large construction projects and points to social transformations that are only very tentatively beginning to be recognized.

The medieval remains demonstrate that the ridge was used again many centuries after the prehistoric settlement had been abandoned. Oued Beht was not simply a single-period settlement but a landscape repeatedly selected by different communities across millennia.

As research continues, this location may become key to understanding how societies in the Maghreb evolved from early farming communities to the medieval rural world.

Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Giulio Lucarini, Cyprian Broodbank, and Toby C. Wilkinson. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

This rainbow-hued rocky plain looks like the landscape of an alien world. And, it turns out, it is.

In this image, we can see an ancient, rocky hill on Mars. In the Red Planet's Southern Highlands, this alien terrain is chock-full of minerals, which we can see clearly defined in this color-enhanced view of the region.

This image was snapped by the HiRISE camera aboard NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), which has been studying the planet's surface, atmosphere and climate since arriving in Martian orbit in March 2006.

But this isn't exactly what the surface of the planet would look like through our eyes; the image is color-enhanced. Why would scientists take a natural-color image and turn it rainbow? Doing so enhances the slight color differences in these rocks, allowing researchers to pick out the different minerals.

As pointed to above, enhancing colors in scientific images can be an incredibly useful tool for exploration.

For instance, in this image, the blue- and green-toned rocks could be full of minerals like pyroxenes and olivine, according to scientists analyzing the image. And they think that the yellow, orange and red patches may contain minerals formed by past interactions with liquid water.

By exploring the mineral content of rocks like this, researchers can peel back the layers of history within the Martian bedrock. The discovery of certain minerals, for example, can show that water flowed on Mars long ago, pointing to potentially habitable conditions.

So, as we can see, this striking rainbow image isn't just a beautiful landscape; it's also hiding serious clues to Mars' history.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. #589. NASA Releases MAX POWER Key Events for Media, Participants

America’s newest aerospace expo and air show – MAX POWER – is fast approaching, and NASA has announced key events beginning Friday, Nov. 6, and running through Sunday, Nov. 8, hosted on and near the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Through multiple park experiences at MAX POWER, NASA and a variety of external collaborators will showcase the newest aircraft, autonomous vehicles, technologies, and more defining the future of air and space. NASA will display its quiet supersonic X-59 plane, and agency partners will showcase Moon rovers, spacecraft, and more. The expo also is a culmination of the agency’s recent Inspiration Tour, which included numerous flyovers to highlight NASA’s fleet of aircraft.

A current schedule of events is available on the agency’s website.

MAX POWER includes opportunities to meet leadership, astronauts, engineers, scientists, and other subject matter experts during the family-friendly public events with gates opening at 9 a.m. EST on Nov. 7 and Nov. 8.

NASA also will share multiple news updates during the weekend, including hosting a news conference at 5 p.m. on Nov. 7, to provide its latest Moon Base update. Located near the lunar South Pole, the Moon Base is humanity’s first outpost for long-term lunar exploration.

#588. Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins

An ancient ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging a long-standing theory about where the ancestors of modern apes, including humans, first evolved. The remarkable find suggests that a crucial chapter of our evolutionary history may have unfolded much farther north than scientists previously believed.

The newly identified species, named Masripithecus moghraensis, lived approximately 17 to 18 million years ago during the Early Miocene. Its fossilized remains were recovered from Wadi Moghra in northern Egypt, making it the first definitive fossil ape ever discovered in North Africa.

The discovery, described in a study published March 26, 2026, in Science, comes from an international team at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center (Egypt) and the University of Southern California (USA). Their findings suggest that northern Africa and the Middle East may have played a central role in the emergence of the evolutionary lineage that eventually gave rise to all living apes.

A Missing Piece of the Ape Evolutionary Puzzle

For decades, scientists believed that early apes and their close relatives were concentrated primarily in regions farther south in Africa. Fossil sites in North Africa had produced remains of ancient monkeys from the Early Miocene, but researchers had never found definitive evidence of apes from the same period.

That gap helped shape prevailing theories about ape evolution. Although younger ape fossils have been discovered across Africa, Europe, and Asia, their evolutionary relationships and geographic origins remain subjects of scientific debate.

The newly discovered Egyptian fossil may help explain what was missing from this picture.

"We spent five years searching for this kind of fossil because, when we look closely at the early ape family tree, it becomes clear that something is missing -- and North Africa holds that missing piece," said Hesham Sallam, a paleontologist at Mansoura University and senior author of the study.

The discovery is especially important for understanding the origins of crown Hominoidea, the evolutionary group that includes the last common ancestor of all living apes and its descendants. Today, that group encompasses gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, and humans.

Scientists suspect that the incomplete geographic distribution of ancient fossils has obscured important details about when and where this group first emerged.

An 18-Million-Year-Old Ape With Unusual Teeth

The fossils were uncovered during expeditions in 2023 and 2024 by researchers from the Sallam Lab at Wadi Moghra, a well-known fossil site in northern Egypt.

The team named the species Masripithecus moghraensis. Its genus name combines Masr (مصر), the Arabic name for Egypt, with píthēkos, the Greek word for ape. The species name honors Wadi Moghra, where the fossils were found.

Although the remains consist only of lower jaw material, they contain an unusual combination of anatomical features that distinguishes the animal from other apes of similar age.

The jaw is exceptionally sturdy, with remarkably large canine and premolar teeth. Its molars also have rounded chewing surfaces covered in pronounced textures. These characteristics offer valuable clues about the foods the animal could eat and how it survived in its environment.

Researchers believe Masripithecus primarily consumed fruit but had teeth powerful enough to process tougher foods when necessary. This dietary flexibility may have been an important survival advantage.

"Together, they suggest that Masripithecus was adapted for versatility. The study interprets its chewing anatomy as evidence of a flexible, mainly fruit-based diet, with the ability to process harder foods such as nuts or seeds when needed. This flexibility would have helped Masripithecus to thrive at a time when climatic changes were leading to more pronounced seasonality in northern Africa and Arabia," said Shorouq Al-Ashqar, a researcher at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center and a first author of the study.

As seasonal differences became more pronounced, the availability of certain foods likely changed throughout the year. An ape capable of eating a wider range of foods would have been better equipped to cope with those fluctuations.

A Discovery That Challenges the Ape Family Tree

The importance of Masripithecus extends well beyond its unusual anatomy. When researchers examined where the species belonged on the evolutionary family tree, they uncovered a surprising result.

Their analysis suggests that Masripithecus was more closely related to living apes than any known ape species from the Early Miocene of East Africa.

To investigate these relationships, the team used advanced statistical techniques known as Bayesian methods. These approaches allow scientists to compare different evolutionary possibilities and estimate how strongly the available evidence supports each one.

The researchers combined anatomical information from living and extinct apes with genetic evidence from living species. They also incorporated the geological ages of fossil specimens, helping them estimate when different evolutionary branches separated.

By bringing these sources of evidence together, the scientists reconstructed relationships among ancient and modern apes and explored where their shared ancestors may have lived.

The results challenge the long-standing assumption that the evolutionary roots of all living apes were centered in or around East Africa.

Could North Africa Be the Birthplace of Modern Apes?

Additional analyses of ancient animal distributions pointed toward northern Africa and the Middle East as the most likely geographic home of the common ancestor of all living apes.

That ancestor is estimated to have lived during the Early Miocene, an interval spanning roughly 23 million to 16 million years ago. This was an important period in primate evolution, when early ape lineages were diversifying, and environments were undergoing substantial changes.

Geography may help explain why this region was so important.

Millions of years ago, Africa, Arabia, and Asia were moving toward a new geological arrangement. As the African and Arabian tectonic plates traveled northward and approached the final stages of their collision with Asia, the connections between these landmasses began to change.

Sea levels also rose and fell, periodically reducing the stretches of water that separated different regions. At certain times, these changes made it easier for animals to move between Africa and Eurasia.

Northern Africa and the Middle East therefore occupied a potentially crucial position in the movement and evolution of ancient mammals, including apes.

The discovery of Masripithecus helps connect previously separated fossil records from Africa and Eurasia. Its presence suggests that apes were already evolving into distinct forms in this region before new land connections made it possible for them to expand into Europe and Asia.

Rather than being a peripheral location in ape evolution, the region may have been an important center of evolutionary diversification.

Scientists Rethink Where Our Ancient Ape Ancestors Lived

The findings have even prompted some of the researchers to reconsider ideas they held throughout their careers.

Erik Seiffert, a paleontologist at the University of Southern California and co-author of the study, explained how the evidence has changed his understanding of ape origins.

"For my entire career, I considered it probable that the common ancestor of all living apes lived in or around East Africa. But this new discovery, and our new and novel analyses of hominoid phylogeny and biogeography, now strongly challenge that idea. And, importantly, the likelihood of this scenario doesn't depend on Masripithecus -- but it is very much consistent with it."

Importantly, the researchers are not claiming that Masripithecus was a direct ancestor of humans or even necessarily the direct ancestor of living apes. Instead, its position on the evolutionary family tree provides evidence about where the broader ancestral lineage may have originated.

The distinction matters because humans emerged much later in evolutionary history. The Egyptian fossil offers clues to an earlier stage, when the distant ancestors shared by humans and other living apes were evolving.

The team's findings also suggest that the traditional emphasis on East African fossils may have provided an incomplete view of this much older evolutionary story.

More Evolutionary Secrets May Be Hidden in Egypt

Although the discovery offers compelling new evidence, scientists still have much to learn about Masripithecus and the early history of modern apes.

Only part of the animal's jaw has been recovered, leaving important questions about its overall appearance, body size, movement, and behavior unanswered. Additional fossils could provide a more complete picture of how this ancient species lived and how it relates to other early apes.

The researchers believe that further exploration of North Africa and the Middle East could reveal additional species and help clarify when and where the major branches of the modern ape family tree began to emerge.

For now, Masripithecus moghraensis offers a striking reminder that even fundamental ideas about our distant evolutionary past can change when scientists uncover evidence in places that have received relatively little attention.

A fossil jaw preserved for nearly 18 million years may be helping scientists piece together a chapter of evolutionary history that was missing all along.

On Nov. 2, 2000, the International Space Station welcomed its first long-term residents.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 2, 2000, the International Space Station welcomed its first long-term residents: NASA astronaut Bill Shepherd and two Russian cosmonauts, Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev. The mission was called Expedition 1.

Before this expedition, NASA had launched five, one-week-long Space Shuttle missions to help build the space station and bring up supplies. But this time, the crew would be staying for four and a half months, and they weren't taking the shuttle. Instead, they took a Russian Soyuz spacecraft, and this was the first Soyuz to ever dock at the space station.

During their stay at the space station, they unpacked supplies and installed new equipment, including the first solar arrays. They left on the space shuttle Discovery, which brought up the Expedition 2 crew that would take their place.

As of today, there has been a continuous astronaut presence in space aboard the International Space Station for 26 years. For all of these years, not a day has gone by without someone living in space, orbiting our planet from aboard the space station.

While the ISS was not the first space station, it has been the longest-running space statin by far. This first crew were pioneers, showing how humans could actually live and work aboard this station. This exploratory mission proved that the station could successfully support astronaut crews.

Since this mission 26 years ago, there have been literally hundreds of astronauts from around the world who have flown to and lived aboard the ISS. While NASA has stated that the station might be decommissioned in the coming years, these accomplishments will remain forever in spaceflight history.

#586. Marc Lore’s Wonder bets on Texas, automation and user-built restaurants as it mulls IPO

Less than a decade after its founding, food startup Wonder has seen its footprint and valuation soar.

Still, the company has even more ambitious plans ahead, like a subscription program to let diners run their own "restaurants," an aggressive expansion in Texas and a potential initial public offering.

Created by serial entrepreneur Marc Lore in 2018, Wonder advertises itself as "the best restaurants from across the country, all in one place." Diners can place takeout or delivery orders from its food hall-style locations on the Wonder-branded app or third-party platforms, including Grubhub, which Wonder now owns.

As Lore described it to CNBC, "Wonder is a vertically integrated food technology platform to make great food more accessible."

To achieve its goal, Wonder plans to open locations in urban, suburban and rural areas nationwide and aims to keep prices lower than the cost of delivered groceries. Thanks to its ownership of Grubhub, Wonder customers who order through the startup's app don't have to pay delivery fees, and its menu prices aren't inflated to cover the cost of commission fees to the delivery platform. Plus, Wonder is automating some of its kitchen functions, like assembling salads and bowls and soon sauces and beverages.

The company aims for food preparation and delivery to be fully autonomous by 2040, Lore said.

Now, Wonder has to convince diners its platform built on cost savings and choice makes it worth their while in a competitive industry.

Lore's lofty vision for Wonder has helped the company raise $3.3 billion to date, from investors like DoorDash, Alphabet's venture arm and Gwyneth Paltrow. Its Series D fundraising round earlier this year raised its pre-money valuation to $9 billion — just under sandwich chain Subway's sale price two years ago.

Wonder's next pitch to investors could be on an IPO road show, assuming that the window for companies across industries to go public reopens in the coming months.

"[The mission] is really why I want to go public and raise the capital that it'll take to build that kind of generational business, also to have a public currency to be able to do more M&A," Lore said. "But I can't talk about timing."

Lore's expertise lies in e-commerce, not restaurants.

He helped found the parent company of Diapers.com and sold it in 2010 to Amazon for $545 million. Just six years later, Walmart paid about $3 billion for his follow-up venture, Jet.com. Lore stayed at the retailer until 2021 to accelerate Walmart's e-commerce growth.

Basketball fans might also recognize Lore as an owner of the Minnesota Timberwolves. In 2021, he and baseball legend Alex Rodriguez agreed to buy the team for $1.5 billion, although the deal was not finalized until 2025. Lore recently struck a deal to shrink his investment to a minority stake "to focus on his business," Rodriguez said in a statement in August, referring to Wonder.

Lore's latest startup began with the idea of bringing food delivery to consumers' homes through sprinter vans outfitted with mobile kitchens. The trucks lasted roughly two years before Wonder phased them out in favor of brick-and-mortar locations, which could serve more food options and lower costs.

Lore's successful track record has helped him win over investors for Wonder.

"I joke around at GV that I do enterprise software investing, AI investing and anything that Marc Lore is running as an active CEO," said Dave Munichiello, managing partner of Alphabet's venture capital arm GV, who has known Lore since his Diapers.com days and invested in Jet.com through GV.

Lore himself thinks that his vision is the reason for Wonder's billions of dollars of funding.

"Everybody eats," he said. "It's defensible from AI."

Wonder has spent more than $1 billion on acquisitions, not including the deals where financial details were not disclosed. Its purchases of Grubhub, delivery and logistics provider Relay, meal-kit provider Blue Apron and buzzy New York restaurant concepts have been expensive.

But Lore said he sees a "tremendous total addressable market" for Wonder if it's able to sell high-quality food at accessible prices, particularly in exurban and rural areas with few dining options beyond fast food and gas stations.

From Virginia to Massachusetts, 170 Wonder storefronts have appeared over the last three years. Next year, the company plans to enter Texas for the first time — with a goal of at least 100 locations in the state by the end of 2027.

Wonder prepares its food at commissary kitchens, then transports it to each individual location, where employees unseal, cook and finish the menu items. Its storefronts are all electric, without gas or venting, so Wonder can quickly move into a new space and cut down on renovations and red tape.

Its locations serve menu items from more than two dozen "restaurants," including Dabba Indian Kitchen, Tejas Barbecue and Pop Salad. Celebrity chefs including Bobby Flay, Michael Symon and Marcus Samuelsson receive up-front payments and equity in Wonder to let the company use their names for some of those concepts. More recent additions include acquisitions such as Blue Ribbon Fried Chicken and Salt Hank's, brands with established followings.

With its wide variety of options housed under one roof, Wonder has drawn comparisons to ghost kitchens, the once-buzzy startups without dine-in seating that flamed out as food delivery orders fell after the Covid pandemic. Once considered a potential disruptor to the restaurant industry, ghost kitchen companies such as Kitchen United have sought bankruptcy protection and wound down their operations.

"You can see there's a front of house [in the] brick and mortar," he said. "You'll see people at lunchtime, sitting there enjoying lunch, so it's not ghost-y in that way. But I think it's also just in the fact that we're vertically integrated."

Wonder has never marketed itself as a ghost kitchen, instead calling itself "a new kind of food hall" or a "modern food court" before landing on a "vertically integrated food technology platform."

Starting Nov. 17, the company plans to take the next step with Wonder Create. Influencers, entrepreneurs and brands can pay $10 a month to start their own "restaurant" based out of a Wonder location and earn a portion of the revenue from orders. Artificial intelligence will help them make their brand, including name, logo, pricing and recipes.

"It could be a restaurant for you and your friends, or you could be an influencer that has a following," Lore said.

He wants Wonder Create to democratize restaurant ownership — minus the capital, overhead costs or oversight of kitchen operations. The platform will eventually be available to the public, with users deciding menu items based on Wonder's pantry.

Besides Wonder Create, the company is also using AI for another initiative. MEL, a proprietary AI platform, can use a customer's health information, like data from an Oura ring or Whoop tracker or even blood biomarkers, to prepare breakfast, lunch and dinner for its user.

MEL is not currently available to Wonder customers, although Lore uses AI to advise his own meals, like the chicken muffin he ate for breakfast on a Tuesday in October.

While Wonder has won over venture capitalists, the battle for diners' stomachs and wallets is tougher.

Budget-conscious consumers have been dining out less often and becoming pickier when they do so. And while food delivery is still more popular than it was before the pandemic, consumers have pulled back on delivery orders compared with their Covid-era peak. Fees and high menu prices, which offset eateries' commission fees with apps, make delivery even more expensive than dining at a restaurant.

Plus, some consumers are skeptical about Wonder more specifically. Posts on social media decry the company's food quality and its funding from venture capital.

"It's OK, but it's just average," Amir Ings, a 27-year-old living in Philadelphia, said in a TikTok reviewing an order of three tacos from Wonder in late 2025. "My expectations were already in the gutter — it's not as bad as I thought it was going to be, but it's still not great. And I paid like $16 for this, but it should have been no more than $8."

Lore told CNBC that Wonder receives thousands of reviews every day from customers, rating the taste, temperature and portion size of their orders on a scale from 1 to 10. Wonder starts its board meetings by talking about taste scores, Munichiello said.

"We're maniacally focused on food quality .... We're constantly iterating on the meals that score lower, and see over time, the last 12 months, our taste scores have improved, our Google reviews have improved," Lore said. "I do expect food quality to improve as we scale, which is not always the case."

Despite lackluster reviews on social media, Wonder has fans. Based on transaction data from Indagari, Wonder had a higher weighted average retention rate — how likely a diner is to return — and higher lifetime value — how much a customer has spent over time — than Cava and Sweetgreen.

Plus, Wonder has succeeded with locations in the most competitive markets for restaurants in the country.

"They made this company work well in the hardest place in the country to stand up this model: New York," Munichiello said. "You have so much choice in New York."

Ultimately, Wonder wants to win over the rest of the U.S. — and public market investors.

In March, the company hired Gabrielle Scheibe Rabinovitch, previously at payment processor Worldpay, as its chief financial officer as it prepares to go public.

Lore declined to comment on the timing of a potential IPO to CNBC, although he has previously told Fortune that the company will be "ready and prepared to go public early next year."

Since buying Blue Apron and Grubhub, Wonder has been operating at a financial loss, The Information previously reported. It plans to bring down the price of its meals by leaning into automation and drone delivery. In the long term, that plan could cut costs, although laying the groundwork won't be cheap.

In recent years, investors have grown less tolerant of startups pursuing growth at all costs, according to Avery Marquez, director of investment strategies at Renaissance Capital. To sway investors, unprofitable companies have to show they are taking steps toward profitability — or that the growth will continue long after the IPO.

#584. Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease

A pesticide used for decades in agriculture may be linked to a much greater risk of Parkinson's disease, and scientists have uncovered a possible explanation for how it damages the brain.

Researchers at UCLA Health found that people with long-term residential exposure to chlorpyrifos, a widely used pesticide, had more than 2.5 times the risk of developing Parkinson's disease compared with those who were not exposed. Laboratory experiments also revealed how the chemical can interfere with the brain's ability to remove damaged proteins, leading to the loss of nerve cells essential for controlling movement.

The study, published in Molecular Neurodegeneration, goes beyond identifying a connection between pesticide exposure and Parkinson's. By examining what happens inside affected brain cells, the researchers uncovered a biological mechanism that could eventually provide new ways to protect the brain from damage.

A Common Pesticide With a Troubling Link to Parkinson's

Parkinson's disease affects nearly one million Americans. The progressive neurological condition gradually damages brain cells involved in movement, often causing tremors, muscle stiffness, slowed movement, and difficulties with coordination.

One of the defining features of Parkinson's is the loss of neurons that produce dopamine. This chemical messenger allows nerve cells to communicate and helps the brain coordinate smooth, controlled movements. As dopamine levels decline, the brain becomes less capable of regulating those movements.

Although inherited genetic factors can influence who develops Parkinson's, researchers have increasingly focused on environmental exposures that may also contribute to the disease. Pesticides are of particular interest because some chemicals used to kill insects or other agricultural pests can also interfere with biological processes in the nervous system.

Chlorpyrifos has been used extensively in agriculture for decades. Its residential use was banned in the United States in 2001, and agricultural applications faced additional restrictions in 2021. However, the pesticide remains in use on many crops in the United States and continues to be widely applied in other countries.

Because exposure may have occurred years before symptoms appeared, understanding the potential long-term effects of chlorpyrifos is particularly important. Identifying specific chemicals associated with Parkinson's could help researchers develop prevention strategies and determine whether previously exposed individuals might benefit from additional neurological monitoring.

Researchers Find More Than Double the Parkinson's Risk

To investigate the connection, UCLA scientists examined information from 829 people diagnosed with Parkinson's disease and 824 people without the condition. All participants were enrolled in the university's long-running Parkinson's Environment and Genes study, which investigates how environmental exposures and inherited factors influence Parkinson's risk.

The researchers combined California's detailed pesticide application records with participants' residential and workplace address histories. This allowed them to estimate how much chlorpyrifos individuals may have encountered over time based on where they lived and worked.

The results revealed a striking association. People with prolonged residential exposure to chlorpyrifos had more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease compared with those who had no such exposure.

Although this population analysis could not establish that the pesticide directly caused Parkinson's, the researchers took an additional step to investigate whether chlorpyrifos could produce the kinds of brain damage seen in people with the disease.

The team exposed mice to chlorpyrifos in aerosol form for 11 weeks. The inhalation approach was designed to resemble a common way people may encounter pesticides in the environment.

The exposed mice developed movement difficulties and lost neurons responsible for producing dopamine. This was particularly significant because the degeneration of these same nerve cells is a central feature of Parkinson's disease.

The researchers also detected inflammation in the animals' brains, along with abnormal accumulations of a protein called alpha-synuclein.

Under normal conditions, alpha-synuclein is found in nerve cells and plays a role in their functioning. However, the protein can accumulate in abnormal clumps that are closely associated with Parkinson's disease. These deposits are a major focus of research into why certain brain cells gradually deteriorate.

Together, the findings showed that chlorpyrifos exposure could reproduce several important characteristics of Parkinson's in laboratory animals, strengthening the biological evidence behind the human population findings.

Scientists Uncover a Breakdown in the Brain's Cleanup System

The researchers then turned to zebrafish to investigate exactly how chlorpyrifos harms neurons. These small fish are frequently used in neuroscience research because they allow scientists to study biological processes involved in nerve cell development and survival.

Their experiments pointed to a disruption in autophagy, a natural cellular maintenance process that helps remove damaged proteins and other unwanted material.

Autophagy functions much like an internal recycling system. Cells use it to break down worn-out or defective components so that potentially harmful material does not accumulate. This process is especially important for neurons, many of which must remain functional throughout a person's lifetime.

When chlorpyrifos interfered with this cleanup system, damaged material accumulated inside neurons, contributing to their deterioration.

The researchers also made an encouraging discovery. When they restored the cellular cleanup process or removed synuclein protein in their experiments, the neurons were protected from damage.

This finding suggests that the pesticide's harmful effects may depend partly on a biological pathway that researchers could potentially target with future treatments.

A Potential New Strategy for Protecting Against Parkinson's

The discovery raises the possibility of developing therapies that strengthen the brain's cellular cleanup mechanisms and help protect vulnerable neurons. Such treatments might eventually prove useful for people exposed to chlorpyrifos or other pesticides that disrupt similar processes.

However, the protective effects have so far been demonstrated in laboratory models. Additional research will be needed to determine whether enhancing autophagy can prevent or reduce pesticide-related brain damage in humans.

Scientists also want to investigate whether other commonly used pesticides interfere with the same cellular mechanisms. Although chlorpyrifos use has declined in the United States, many people were exposed before restrictions were introduced, and related agricultural chemicals remain widely used.

The findings could also help identify people with a history of substantial pesticide exposure who may benefit from closer neurological monitoring. Earlier recognition of possible changes in brain function could become increasingly important as researchers work toward treatments that slow or prevent Parkinson's progression.

Dr. Jeff Bronstein, professor of Neurology at UCLA Health and the study's senior author, emphasized the importance of identifying a particular chemical rather than treating all pesticides as a single category.

"This study establishes chlorpyrifos as a specific environmental risk factor for Parkinson's disease, not just pesticides as a general class," said Dr. Jeff Bronstein.

"By showing the biological mechanism in animal models, we've demonstrated that this association is likely causal. The discovery that autophagy dysfunction drives the neurotoxicity also points us toward potential therapeutic strategies to protect vulnerable brain cells."

#583. 30,000-year-old DNA reveals Ice Age Europeans were far more connected than we thought

More than 30,000 years ago, people living across Ice Age Europe were far more connected than scientists previously believed. New genetic evidence reveals unexpected links between populations separated by enormous distances, challenging the long-held idea that eastern and western European groups remained largely isolated from one another.

An international research team led by the University of Vienna made the discovery by analyzing ancient DNA from rare human remains and traces of human genetic material preserved in cave sediments. Published in Science Advances, the findings provide a new picture of how prehistoric Europeans interacted, exchanged genes, and maintained populations through thousands of years of dramatic environmental change.

The research focuses on people associated with one of Europe's major Paleolithic cultures (the Gravettian), which flourished across the continent roughly 34,000 to 25,000 years ago. Archaeological discoveries have long suggested that these ancient populations maintained connections over considerable distances. However, previous genetic evidence pointed to relatively distinct eastern and western ancestry groups.

By combining new genetic findings with previously collected DNA, researchers uncovered evidence that these groups were more interconnected than expected. They also found signs that certain populations in southwestern Europe maintained their genetic ancestry for thousands of years.

A Woman From 30,000 Years Ago Reveals Hidden Genetic Connections

One of the most revealing discoveries came from the remains of a woman who lived approximately 30,000 years ago in what is now southwestern France. Found at Isturitz Cave, her remains provided the oldest genome-wide genetic dataset yet obtained from a modern human in southwestern Europe.

Her DNA contained a surprising combination of ancestry. Although most of her genetic background was associated with western European populations, she also carried ancestry linked to people from central and eastern Europe.

Using genetic modeling, researchers estimated that this mixing between populations occurred approximately 32,500 to 31,500 years ago. The finding suggests that genetic connections extended across large portions of Europe much earlier than scientists had previously established.

"Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed," says first author Pere Gelabert, Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna. "Gene flow across such large distances adds a new dimension to our understanding of how Gravettian populations were connected."

The researchers identified a similar genetic signature in another ancient individual whose remains had previously been studied at Ormesson, France. Combined with archaeological discoveries, the evidence strengthens the possibility that Isturitz Cave served as a gathering place where different groups of prehistoric people encountered one another.

Ancient DNA Hidden in Cave Sediments Reveals Ice Age Survival

While some ancient Europeans exchanged genes across considerable distances, other populations appear to have maintained a continuous genetic presence in particular regions for thousands of years.

Evidence from Chufín Cave in northern Spain suggests that ancestry associated with western European populations persisted in southwestern Europe over an extended period.

The researchers also used an increasingly valuable technique that allows scientists to recover human DNA directly from cave sediments, even when no identifiable human remains are present. Tiny traces of genetic material left behind by ancient inhabitants can survive in soil and other deposits for thousands of years, providing information about people whose bones have never been found.

At El Mirón Cave in Cantabria, Spain, the team recovered human nuclear DNA from a sediment layer dating back approximately 22,000 years. Despite finding no human bones or teeth in the layer, they obtained enough genetic information to determine the ancestry of the people who had occupied the site.

"Sedimentary DNA allows us to recover genetic information from periods where human remains are missing," says senior author Ron Pinhasi, Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna, whose team led this study. "This gives us a way to connect archaeological layers with the genetic ancestry of the people who occupied a site."

The results indicate that western European ancestry persisted in the region through the Last Glacial Maximum, a period when enormous ice sheets reached their greatest extent during the last Ice Age.

This supports the idea that the Iberian Peninsula, which includes present-day Spain and Portugal, served as an important refuge for prehistoric humans during some of the coldest conditions of the Ice Age.

Ancient Mother and Son Offer Clues About Prehistoric Mating

Another revealing discovery came from southern Italy, where researchers examined the genetic remains of Ostuni1b, a male fetus believed to be the son of a previously studied woman known as Ostuni1.

Genetic analysis suggests that the child's father likely belonged to the same ancestral population as his mother. However, the parents were not closely related, offering evidence that mating patterns within these ancient communities may have helped limit inbreeding.

This finding adds another dimension to the emerging picture of prehistoric European societies. Even as some populations maintained relatively stable genetic ancestry within their home regions, they could also participate in broader networks of genetic exchange spanning considerable distances.

Together, the discoveries show that long-term regional continuity and widespread genetic connections were not mutually exclusive. Both helped shape the population history of Ice Age Europe.

Building on these results, Gelabert and his colleagues are now combining DNA recovered from ancient sediments with advanced proteomic techniques, which examine proteins for clues about past life. Their goal is to investigate the earliest expansions of modern humans across Europe, including how these populations interacted with carnivores in places where bones and other organic remains are scarce.

#580. FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, alleging retailer overcharged shoppers

The Federal Trade Commission said Monday that it filed a lawsuit along with 20 states accusing Dollar General of charging customers more than the prices it displays on shelves, price tags and in advertisements.

Shares of Dollar General dropped about 4% after the FTC announced the lawsuit.

The complaint alleges that thousands of Dollar General stores have "taken advantage of vulnerable shoppers by extracting millions of dollars in unlawful overcharges with insufficient safeguards to prevent the practice."

It also argues that Dollar General has received "tens of thousands" of complaints from consumers about charging higher than advertised prices, but that it has not implemented policies to address the problem.

The states joining the FTC in the lawsuit are Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.

"Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last," said Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection.

Dollar General issued a statement in response to the lawsuit, saying it will "defend this litigation vigorously."

"As with other retailers and despite our policies and procedures, occasional price discrepancies can occur," the statement read. "When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement."

Dollar General's statement said that it has cooperated with the FTC's investigation since February and has produced documents, data and sworn testimony. In September, the FTC sent a draft complaint and settlement offer. The company said it had sent a monetary counteroffer and was surprised when the FTC filed the lawsuit rather than responding to the offer.

The suit comes as shoppers look for discounts while they face elevated food and gas prices. Officials across the political spectrum also aim to show their efforts to protect consumers from high costs ahead of the midterm election next week.

#579. Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists

Scientists have proposed a surprising new explanation for why the universe exists, and it centers on a mysterious particle that physicists have largely overlooked for decades. Their theory suggests this forgotten particle may have played a crucial role in shaping the early cosmos and allowing matter to survive after the Big Bang.

The research addresses one of the most fundamental mysteries in physics: why does the universe contain matter instead of nothing at all? Scientists believe matter and antimatter were produced in nearly equal amounts in the early universe. When these opposites encounter one another, they annihilate and release energy. If they had existed in perfectly equal quantities, virtually all matter could have disappeared, leaving no material to form stars, planets, or life.

Now, researchers from the University of Southampton and the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur believe they may have found an important piece of the puzzle. Their explanation involves a little-understood relative of the neutrino, an extremely lightweight particle that rarely interacts with ordinary matter.

A Forgotten Particle With a Powerful Role in the Early Universe

The team focused on a type of particle known as a 'decoupled' heavy neutrino. Unlike ordinary neutrinos, this hypothetical heavier relative has generally been considered too weakly connected to other particles to significantly influence the universe.

However, the researchers found that its unusually long lifetime could have made it far more important than previously thought. According to their calculations, the particle may have survived long enough to temporarily dominate the universe's energy density as the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang.

That brief period of dominance could have altered how the early universe evolved, influencing the conditions that ultimately allowed matter to outnumber antimatter.

Dr. Rishav Roshan of the University of Southampton, an author of the study, explained:

"This decoupled heavy neutrino has long been dismissed as an irrelevant background detail in particle physics.

"However, it decays incredibly slowly. As the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang, the particle lived long enough that it temporarily took over the energy density of the universe and triggered a matter-dominated period."

The findings were published in Physical Review Letters, a scientific journal of the American Physical Society.

How a Heavy Neutrino Could Explain Why Matter Survived

Previous attempts to explain why matter prevailed over antimatter generally left out the decoupled heavy neutrino. Because it interacts so weakly with other particles, scientists assumed it would have little influence on the processes responsible for creating the imbalance.

The new research challenges that assumption. The team found that even a particle with extremely weak interactions could indirectly affect the conditions under which matter gained its crucial advantage.

This imbalance, known as matter and antimatter asymmetry, is essential to understanding our existence. For reasons physicists are still trying to explain, the early universe ended up with slightly more matter than antimatter. That small difference allowed some matter to remain after most particles and their antiparticles annihilated one another.

"The fact that we are here at all proves that an asymmetry between matter and antimatter occurred," added Dr. Roshan.

"The decoupled neutrino shifted the temperature in the early universe at which fundamental particles - like electrons and other leptons - interacted with their anti-particles with the help of Standard Model Higgs boson.

"This temperature acts like a switch that shapes how the matter-antimatter imbalance was built up."

The Higgs boson is a fundamental particle associated with the mechanism that gives many elementary particles their mass. In the researchers' proposed scenario, the heavy neutrino changed the temperature conditions governing important particle interactions involving the Higgs boson.

By shifting when these interactions occurred, the particle could have influenced how the imbalance between matter and antimatter developed. In other words, something long considered insignificant may have helped determine why the universe contains matter at all.

Ancient Gravitational Waves Could Reveal the Answer

The theory could also have important implications for understanding how the universe expanded in its earliest stages.

Study co-author Dr. Sudipta Show of the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur said the findings suggest that the forgotten particle may have dramatically altered the expansion history of the young cosmos.

He added: "It offers us a new explanation for how matter won.

"The dramatic shift in the early expansion of the cosmos leaves distinct but detectable imprints of changes, for example on primordial gravitational waves.

"These gravitational wave signatures open up new avenues for us to unravel the evolution of the early universe after the Big Bang."

Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of space and time. Scientists believe processes in the extremely early universe may have generated primordial gravitational waves that carry information about conditions from that distant era.

According to the new theory, the temporary dominance of the heavy neutrino could have left recognizable signatures in those ancient signals. Detecting such patterns could eventually provide a way to investigate whether the proposed particle really influenced the universe's earliest evolution.

For now, the explanation remains theoretical. But it offers physicists a new possibility for solving one of cosmology's deepest mysteries: how matter survived when its encounter with antimatter could have left the universe almost entirely empty.

#578. Pennsylvania’s Grand Canyon

Amid the warm hues of fall foliage, Pine Creek Gorge forms a deep scar in the Allegheny Plateau.

North-central Pennsylvania is canyon country with an Appalachian flair. Pine Creek Gorge reaches depths of about 1,500 feet (460 meters) along its gently curving path through the forests of the Allegheny Plateau. Instead of the steep rock walls characteristic of canyons in the desert Southwest, lushly vegetated slopes outline the dramatic topography. In autumn, greens give way to a palette of reds and golds sought out by leaf peepers.

Nicknamed the “Grand Canyon of Pennsylvania,” the gorge runs for some 45 miles (72 kilometers) from Ansonia south to Pine Creek’s confluence with the West Branch Susquehanna River, reaching its greatest depths around Waterville. The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on the NASA-USGS Landsat 8 satellite captured this image of Pine Creek Gorge on October 25, 2026, when colorful fall foliage was on display.

Glaciers played a key role in the canyon’s formation, though ice itself did not carve it. Pine Creek once flowed to the north, opposite of what it does today. As glaciers advanced into the region from the northeast during the last ice age, they dammed the river and filled the valley with lakes. Those lakes eventually overflowed, sending water streaming to the south.

When the ice receded, Pine Creek was already becoming entrenched in its southward course. Rocks and sand left behind by the melting ice further prevented the water from turning back north. Glacial meltwater continued to rush through the valley, deepening and shaping it into its current form.

Today, the hillsides around the gorge are blanketed in northern hardwood and mixed oak forest, sprinkled with hemlock and white pine. In autumn, the deciduous trees impart red and gold hues to the landscape akin to the rock of the famous Arizona canyon.

This seasonal change around Pine Creek Gorge has not always been so visually pleasing. With increasing demand for wood products in early 19th-century America, loggers found their way to the area’s stately trees. At the time, white pine and hemlock several feet in diameter and towering hardwoods populated the slopes around Pine Creek Gorge. The pines were especially valued for making ship masts, and hemlock bark was used to tan leather. Before railroads, logs were floated down Pine Creek to the Susquehanna in massive drives. By the early 20th century, decades of logging left the land so barren that the area earned the moniker “Pennsylvania Desert.”

The forest has since returned, and with it, wild inhabitants such as black bears, coyotes, bobcats, timber rattlesnakes, and a diversity of songbirds. In 1968, an area of 30,000 acres (12,000 hectares) was designated a National Natural Landmark. Visitors can experience the gorge’s natural splendor at many points along its path, including from multiple state parks and the Pine Creek Rail Trail.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Photo by fishhawk, via Flickr. Story by Lindsey Doermann.

These glacial landforms jut into northern Lake Huron, surrounded by sheltered channels and coves frequented by fish and small watercraft.

#576. NASA's Hubble and Webb discover ancient worlds that remember their past

NASA's Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have uncovered surprising clues about the earliest days of our solar system by examining some of the smallest and faintest objects ever observed beyond Neptune. The findings challenge expectations about how planets form and suggest that these distant, icy bodies have preserved evidence of their origins for billions of years.

For the first time, astronomers combined observations from Hubble and Webb to investigate trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs), tiny bodies that travel around the Sun far beyond Neptune's orbit. Researchers discovered 27 previously unknown objects, but their findings revealed an unexpected puzzle. There were fewer small objects than some theories predicted, and their colors closely resembled those of much larger objects in the same distant regions.

These frozen remnants offer a rare opportunity to study the materials that eventually became planets. Most are extraordinarily difficult to detect, shining more than 100 million times more faintly than objects visible to the naked eye. Two related studies published in The Astronomical Journal examined the newly identified objects to learn more about their sizes, compositions, and ancient history.

Ancient Building Blocks of the Solar System

Scientists believe planets began forming when tiny particles of dust and pebbles orbiting the young Sun gradually accumulated into larger bodies. Over time, these materials formed objects roughly the size of cities, known as "planetesimals." These early building blocks eventually combined to create the planets we see today.

However, that final stage of growth did not occur for many objects beyond Neptune. Instead of developing into full-sized planets, countless smaller bodies remained, preserving evidence of the solar system's earliest period of formation.

To investigate these distant survivors, research teams led by PhD candidates at the University of Victoria in Canada, working under the guidance of the National Research Council of Canada, and Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff conducted the deepest survey of trans-Neptunian objects to date. Both space telescopes observed the same region of sky simultaneously, with Hubble collecting visible light and Webb capturing infrared light.

By combining these observations, astronomers could examine the objects' colors, estimate their sizes, and determine how they orbit the Sun. Their colors are especially valuable because they provide clues about the chemical makeup of their surfaces, much like fingerprints that reveal an object's identity and history.

The researchers focused on two distinct populations of trans-Neptunian objects, known as dynamically "cold" and dynamically "hot" TNOs. These descriptions refer to their orbital behavior rather than their temperatures.

Cold objects have largely remained in the regions where they originally formed. They follow relatively circular paths around the Sun and stay close to the plane in which most of the solar system's planets orbit.

Hot objects have experienced a much more turbulent history. They originally formed between the present-day orbits of Uranus and Neptune but were scattered outward as the giant planets shifted positions early in the solar system's development. Their current orbits are much more elongated, and they travel above and below the solar system's main orbital plane.

Despite these dramatically different histories, the two populations revealed an unexpected similarity. Even the smallest objects appear to have retained surface characteristics resembling those of their larger counterparts.

Tiny Worlds Preserve Their Ancient Origins

Before the observations, scientists suspected that smaller TNOs would show clear evidence of repeated collisions over billions of years. Impacts could have fractured the objects and exposed fresh material, potentially changing their surface compositions and colors.

Instead, the newly discovered objects displayed the same general color relationships seen among larger TNOs. This suggests that collisions may have altered their surfaces much less than expected.

One possibility is that these objects have experienced fewer impacts than astronomers previously assumed. Another is that their surfaces somehow retain their original compositions even after collisions. Researchers have not yet determined which explanation is correct.

"You could imagine a scenario where getting knocked around and fragmented would change the surface composition, and then you would see a different surface color for tiny TNOs compared to their larger siblings. So it's really fascinating to see that the smallest objects are somehow 'remembering' and preserving the history of how they were made," said Northern Arizona University PhD candidate Anastasia Morgan, who led the study of color and composition.

"These dynamically 'hot' TNOs retain a signature of where they were born, even though they've been orbitally scrambled since then," said co-author David Trilling of Northern Arizona University.

The observations indicate that both hot and cold TNOs have maintained color patterns linked to their formation, with surprisingly little apparent change since the solar system's beginnings. These ancient objects may therefore preserve important information about the environments in which they first took shape.

Webb Finds Fewer Tiny Worlds Than Expected

The James Webb Space Telescope also provided another important piece of the puzzle. Its observations allowed scientists to examine how many objects exist at different sizes, revealing an unexpected resemblance between the two populations.

Although hot and cold TNOs formed in different parts of the early solar system, their overall size distributions were remarkably alike. This suggests that the processes responsible for creating planetesimals may have operated in much the same way across different environments.

"It's very interesting that the process of planetesimal formation ends up producing the same distribution of sizes for both cold and hot populations, despite forming in different regions of the early solar system. The process seems to be insensitive to disk conditions, producing similar planetesimal sizes whether the disk is hot or cold, and dense or fluffy," said University of Victoria PhD candidate Marielle Eduardo, who led the study on size distribution.

The researchers also identified a surprising shortage of very small TNOs compared with predictions from some existing planet formation models. Understanding why fewer objects were detected could help scientists refine their explanations of how the solar system's original building blocks developed.

Webb's extraordinary sensitivity made it possible to discover 27 exceptionally faint objects. One was so dim that detecting it would be comparable to standing on Earth and spotting a small swarm of fireflies on the Moon.

The smallest object measured just 3 miles (5 kilometers) across, making it approximately five times smaller than the objects detectable with even the most sensitive telescopes on the ground.

Hubble and Webb Reveal New Clues to Planet Formation

These discoveries depended on the complementary capabilities of NASA's two powerful space observatories. Hubble's ability to detect visible light and Webb's sensitivity to infrared light gave scientists a more complete picture of the distant objects than either telescope could have provided independently.

Together, the telescopes have opened a new window into a largely unexplored population of ancient solar system remnants. Their surprising similarities, preserved surface characteristics, and unexpected numbers offer important clues about the processes that shaped the planets billions of years ago.

#573. IceCube detects ghost particles with 10 billion times the energy of solar neutrinos

An enormous number of invisible particles are constantly traveling through Earth, passing through our bodies and continuing into space as though almost nothing stands in their way. Known as neutrinos, these mysterious particles are among the most difficult objects in the universe to detect. Yet scientists are finding ways to capture evidence of their passage, opening new opportunities to investigate the cosmos and its most extreme environments.

Neutrino research has played a remarkable role in modern physics. Discoveries involving these particles have contributed to five Nobel Prizes in Physics. This year, physicist Francis Halzen received the prestigious award "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin."

George Fuller, a Distinguished Professor of Physics at the University of California San Diego, has studied nuclear physics, particle astrophysics, and cosmology for decades. He also collaborated with Halzen on an early scientific paper about IceCube. His expertise helps explain what makes neutrinos so unusual and why scientists built an enormous observatory deep within the Antarctic ice to study them.

Neutrinos belong to a group known as elementary particles, which scientists believe have no smaller components. They come in three varieties, called electron, muon, and tau neutrinos. Unlike electrically charged particles, neutrinos have no electric charge. They do have mass, but it is extraordinarily small, potentially around 10 million times less than the mass of an electron. Their exact masses remain unknown, as does the mechanism responsible for producing them.

Another remarkable characteristic is their ability to travel through matter with almost no resistance. Because neutrinos interact so rarely with other particles, they can cross vast distances at speeds approaching the speed of light.

Neutrinos originate from many different places, including the Sun, distant regions of space, and sources scientists have yet to identify. They are also astonishingly abundant. Estimates suggest the universe contains roughly 1089 neutrinos, equivalent to approximately one billion for every atom in existence.

"Neutrinos are truly ghost-like particles," stated Fuller. "It's hard to stop them. It's hard to catch them. How do we even know they exist or where they are?"

Ghost Particles That Pass Through Almost Anything

Despite their elusive nature, neutrinos occasionally interact with matter through a fundamental force known as the weak interaction. This force is approximately 20 orders of magnitude weaker than electromagnetism. Such interactions can cause neutrinos to scatter or be absorbed, providing scientists with a way to detect them. However, these events are so uncommon that observing them requires exceptionally sensitive equipment.

Their ability to move through dense material also makes neutrinos valuable messengers from otherwise inaccessible regions of the universe. They can escape from environments surrounding collapsing stars and black holes, carrying information that other forms of radiation might not reveal.

The scale of this invisible activity is staggering. Approximately 100 billion neutrinos pass through every square centimeter of your body each second, almost entirely unnoticed.

"Because the interaction is so weak, neutrinos can get through almost anything," said Fuller. "Light years of lead -- depending on their energy, they would go right through it."

How Scientists Learned to Detect Neutrinos

The search for neutrinos began long before technology existed to observe them. During the 1930s, physicist Wolfgang Pauli proposed that an unknown particle might explain why energy appeared to be missing during certain forms of radioactive decay. He initially used a different name for the hypothetical particle (he called them "neutrons" at the time).

Pauli understood how difficult it would be to verify his idea. He famously acknowledged the problem by saying, "I have done a terrible thing, I have postulated a particle that cannot be detected."

For decades, neutrinos remained beyond the reach of experiments. That changed in 1956, when physicists Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines successfully detected them in an experiment known as "Project Poltergeist."

The breakthrough established that neutrinos were real, but detecting them remained an enormous challenge. Scientists needed increasingly sophisticated instruments to investigate the rarest and most energetic neutrinos arriving from space.

Why Antarctica Is Ideal for Hunting Cosmic Neutrinos

During the 1990s, Halzen recognized that the South Pole offered an extraordinary natural environment for neutrino research. Far below Antarctica's surface, immense volumes of ice are exceptionally clear, with relatively few bubbles or contaminants to interfere with the detection of faint flashes of light.

His vision eventually led to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a gigantic scientific instrument embedded within roughly one cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice. To construct it, researchers drilled deep holes and lowered long strings of sensitive light detectors called photomultiplier tubes.

These instruments search for brief flashes of blue light produced through a phenomenon called Cherenkov radiation. The light appears when a neutrino interacts with matter in the ice and produces a charged particle traveling faster than light can move through that material.

By recording these flashes, researchers can identify evidence of neutrinos that would otherwise pass through Earth without leaving a detectable trace.

IceCube is particularly important for studying neutrinos that arrive from distant cosmic sources with extraordinarily high energies. Unlike the enormous quantities of relatively low-energy neutrinos produced by the Sun, these powerful cosmic visitors are extremely rare. The observatory detects only a few dozen of the most energetic examples each year.

When one of these neutrinos interacts with the ice, it can produce a rapidly moving electron or muon. A muon, for example, generates a cone of Cherenkov light as it travels through the ice. Scientists analyze the resulting pattern of light to estimate the neutrino's energy and reconstruct the direction from which it arrived.

For Fuller, these exceptionally energetic neutrinos are among IceCube's most exciting discoveries because their origins and the physical processes responsible for accelerating them remain poorly understood.

"Some ultra-high-energy neutrinos detected at IceCube have roughly 10 billion times the energy of a typical neutrino from the Sun. One detected by a similar experiment has an energy 200 times higher than that. We don't really know where that neutrino came from," he stated. "The fact that it got here at all may be saying something profound about the universe. In that sense, Halzen really is at the frontier of experimental fundamental particle physics."

Neutrinos Could Reveal Secrets of the Big Bang

The scientific effort to understand neutrinos extends far beyond Antarctica. Researchers at UC San Diego are also involved in another major observatory that could offer new insights into these elusive particles and the universe's earliest history.

Located high in Chile's Atacama Desert, the Simons Observatory is gathering information about the cosmic microwave background, the ancient radiation left over from the early universe. Often described as the oldest light in the cosmos, this radiation provides a valuable record of conditions that existed shortly after the Big Bang.

UC San Diego helped establish the observatory, and Brian Keating, a Distinguished Professor of Physics at the university, serves as its principal investigator.

Although the observatory primarily studies ancient light, its measurements can also reveal information about neutrinos from the earliest stages of cosmic history. The project could provide an enormous amount of new data related to these ancient particles, potentially offering insights that other experiments cannot obtain.

Fuller believes the anticipated observations could improve scientists' understanding of the Big Bang, the early evolution of the universe, and other fundamental questions about how the cosmos developed.

"Halzen's work, and the work of those he inspired with his vision, was foundational in giving humanity a new window on the universe and on the mysterious and notoriously slippery neutrino," he stated.

Materials provided by University of California - San Diego. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#572. JetBlue stock surges as company outlook calms investors

JetBlue Airways reported a bigger loss in the third quarter compared with last year, but shares surged as the carrier's upbeat forecast that it will return to profitability appeared to calm investors after a Monday rout.

JetBlue stock rose 18% in trading Tuesday after hitting a new low a day earlier as investors fretted about the company's financial future.

The Monday drop came after the Wall Street Journal reported Friday that a group of the airline's senior creditors is reportedly working with restructuring adviser PJT Partners.

"We have no intention, no plans to file for bankruptcy. We are not engaged with any restructuring company," CEO Joanna Geraghty told CNBC on Tuesday. "We are focused on delivering to our shareholders what we laid out for at the beginning of our turnaround plan."

She said there is a "fundamental disconnect between the narrative in the bond market and what our financial results actually demonstrate."

The New York airline late Monday reported that its revenue per available seat mile, a key metric measuring how much operating revenue a carrier generates for every seat flown one mile, would be up as much as 22% in the fourth quarter, bringing the annual increase to an expected 13.5% to 14.5%

"We're not seeing any meaningful pushback," Geraghty said in the interview.

JetBlue on Monday posted a net loss of $257 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a loss of $143 million a year earlier. The carrier's fuel bill rose 61% to $868 million.

The carrier said it ended the quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.

JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing Monday.

"Importantly, we believe we have the liquidity and financing options to create a strong bridge to at least $1 EPS and positive free cash flow in 2028," CFO Ursula Hurley said in a statement. "We remain focused on disciplined cost execution and capital management as we work toward sustained profitability and positive free cash flow."

Here is what JetBlue reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG:

JetBlue last posted an annual profit in 2019. The airline is in the middle of a multiyear turnaround plan that includes cutting cuts and boosting revenue by investing in premium seats, like a new domestic first class section that recently went on sale.

Fuel costs have eaten into airline profits across the board. JetBlue said travel demand has remained strong despite higher fares.

JetBlue's average fares rose more than 19% to $245.11 in the third quarter from $205.67 in the year-earlier period.

The airline has struggled not just with higher costs but also with competition from larger rivals.

It sought to acquire now-defunct carrier Spirit Airlines, but that deal was upended by a federal judge who ruled it was anticompetitive. A judge also blocked a regional partnership between JetBlue and American Airlines, which the airlines argued would help them compete better against carriers in the congested Northeast U.S. JetBlue now has a partnership with United Airlines.

The carrier expects to grow capacity no more than 4% in the current quarter. One bright spot, executives said, has been expanding at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport, the former home hub of Spirit, which collapsed in May.
